rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · Water in the Tunnels
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a bright mountain stream bursting through a broken tunnel wall into a torchlit goblin cave, comic goblins with big heads and soft bare feet scrambling up rock ledges clutching pots and maps, swirling blue water with golden lantern reflections, a miner boy and bearded miners watching safely from a high dry passage, playful dramatic light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Curdie ran down the mountain in the morning and told the miners everything: the secret channel, the flood, the plan to drown them all. 'Then we shall sing,' said his father Peter, 'and we shall be ready.' So the miners worked and sang louder than ever, and kept their lanterns dry and their barrels high.
The goblins' own channel floods their own halls, while the miners stay dry.

That night the goblins broke through their channel at last, and the mountain stream rushed in. But the water ran the wrong way for the goblins. Down and down it poured, into their halls and houses and kitchens, washing away their maps and giving their soft bare feet the very worst sort of surprise.
New word: channel — a little dug waterway. The goblins dug this one very carefully, and it worked perfectly — in entirely the wrong direction.

Up the goblins scrambled, out of the mountain and away over the hills, so fast that their hard heads rang like kettles. The miners stood in their dry, lantern-lit passage and laughed until the rocks rang too, and Peter the miner laughed loudest of all the miners in the mountain.

But Curdie did not laugh all the way home. In the crowd of scrambling goblins he had seen the goblin king and queen slip away with their little prince, the queen rubbing her great stone shoe and swearing revenge. 'Beaten is not gone,' said Curdie to his father. 'Goblins hold a grudge the way other folk hold a hammer.' And high above them all, in her tower, a grandmother was already spinning a new thread.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Tapping Under the Castle
chapters.artPrompt: a dark stone castle cellar with stacked barrels and crates, a miner boy lying flat on the cold floor with his ear pressed to the stone, his lantern glowing beside him, faint sparks of dust falling from the ceiling where tiny picks tap from below, a nervous old nurse holding a candle on the stairs, deep blue shadows with warm lantern gold, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Winter came, and the castle stood quiet under the snow. But one night the old nurse Lootie came running to the King's captain, white as her apron. 'Tapping,' she said, with her hand on her heart. 'Under the cellars. Tapping, tapping — like little picks.' And she would not go back downstairs alone.

The captain sent for Curdie, for miners know mountain sounds best of anyone. Curdie lay flat on the cellar floor with his ear against the stone, and his face grew very serious indeed. Goblins. Digging up into the castle itself — and he could guess exactly whom they meant to carry away.
Down in the dark cellar, Curdie listens to little picks tapping under the stone.
New word: cellar — a dark room under a house, where castles keep their wine and stores. It was the very last room the goblins should have chosen.

The goblin king's plan was plain to him now. Their flood had failed, so they would come the old way — up through the cellars on a feast night, when the guards were busy and the halls were loud, and steal the princess away for the goblin prince. 'Well,' said Curdie, standing up and brushing his knees, 'feast nights suit me fine. Miners sing on feast nights louder than any day of the year.'

So while the goblins tapped, the castle prepared. Extra guards were set, and barrels were rolled into rows, and Curdie taught every soldier he met the three loudest mining songs in the whole mountain.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · A New Ball of Thread
chapters.artPrompt: a round tower room full of morning light and rose vines, a beautiful silver-haired lady at a spinning wheel holding out a small ball of glowing silver thread to a little golden-haired princess, a birdcage of doves and a bowl of roses nearby, soft pearl and rose colors, gentle dreamy light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Irene did not know about the tapping, but she had a dream she could not forget — of goblin feet, soft and many, coming up out of the floor. So she climbed the tower stair in the morning light to find her grandmother.

The lovely lady was waiting for her, and in her lap lay a new ball of thread, spun finer than the first. 'This is for the dark days coming,' she said. 'Keep it near you, Irene. When you are most afraid, open your hand and follow where it leads. It has never yet brought anyone to harm.'
A new ball of silver thread, finer than the first, waits in the grandmother's lap.
Talk together: the thread only helps if Irene trusts it all the way, even when the way looks dark. Ask your child: what helps you keep going when you cannot see the end?

'And must I tell no one?' asked Irene, remembering the first rule. 'Only the one who needs it with you,' said her grandmother. 'Threads are not for showing, little one. They are for following.' And she kissed Irene, and the round room filled with the smell of roses.
Irene carried the ball in her pocket after that, day and night. It did not weigh anything at all, and it shone very faintly when she was alone, like a star that knows it is wanted.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Night Attack
chapters.artPrompt: a wide torchlit castle cellar where singing miners and soldiers with pickaxes and lanterns face a tumbling crowd of comic goblins covering their ears, a great goblin queen with a huge stone shoe sitting flat on the floor holding her foot, a small princess holding a glowing silver thread beside a miner boy, chaotic joyful golden light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The attack came on a great feast night, when the halls were bright and the guards were busy. Up through the cellars came the goblins — hundreds of them, hard heads down and soft feet silent — till Curdie's song met them at the stair, and stopped half of them where they stood.

Oh, the miners sang that night! Curdie roared, the soldiers bellowed, the cooks joined in with pots for cymbals, and the goblins clapped their hands over their ears and tumbled over each other in the dark like ninepins.
The great cellar fight, won with pickaxes, lanterns, and very loud songs.

The goblin queen came on last, terrible in her great stone shoe, and knocked a guard flat with one stamp of it. But Curdie was ready. He swung his pickaxe with all a miner's strength, and the stone shoe cracked from top to bottom — and the queen sat down on the floor, forgot all about fighting, and had to be carried off by her own family.
New word: pickaxe — a miner's tool with a long handle and a pointed iron head. In this house, it was also a musical instrument, more or less.

Then Peter and the miners opened the water gates, and the last of the mountain stream poured down the goblins' tunnels — and that was the end of the goblins in that mountain, for good and all. The castle stood safe, the princess slept safe, and the miners went home rich in songs.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The King Comes Home
chapters.artPrompt: a great castle hall in winter sunshine where a tall king in a fur cloak lifts a small golden-haired princess into the air laughing, a miner boy and his bearded father standing before the throne, miners and soldiers cheering with lanterns and pickaxes, garlands on the stone pillars, bright warm light through high windows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: When the news reached the King, he came home faster than kings usually travel. He caught Irene up and hugged her till she squeaked, and then he heard the whole story — the tapping, and the thread, and the queen's unlucky shoe — twice through, and asked for it once again.

Then he sent for Curdie and for Peter the miner. 'A boy who listens under floors and sings on staircases,' said the King, 'is worth a whole cabinet of counsellors.' He would have heaped Curdie with gold, but Curdie had one wish only: that every miner in the mountain should be well paid, and well sung about, forever.
The King thanks a miner's boy, while a small princess holds her thread.
New word: reward — something given to thank a person for being brave or good. Curdie's reward was for everybody, which made it the best kind.

So it was ordered, and better still, it was done. And the mountain, hearing the news, sang for a week. The old goblin holes far below heard the singing too, and shivered, and stayed exactly where they were.

The King stayed all that bright winter. He and Irene walked in the snow, and Curdie showed them the miners' paths, and for the first time in years the castle did not feel like a castle. It felt like a home with friends in it.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Light in the Tower
chapters.artPrompt: a castle tower rising into a deep blue starry evening, a warm golden light glowing in its high round window, a boy with a pickaxe on his shoulder and a small princess hand in hand on the stair below among first stars, pine mountains and a quiet snowy village, gentle violet and gold palette, storybook illustration

blocks.text: On the last evening, Irene took Curdie's hand. 'There is someone who must thank you too,' she said. So up the tower stair they went, higher than Curdie had ever climbed in his life, to the round room where the roses hung.

But Curdie saw only a great plain room, empty and dusty, with the wind in the chimney. Irene saw her grandmother, silver and beautiful, and the spinning wheel, and the lamp that never goes out. He rubbed his eyes and rubbed them again, and still saw nothing at all.
The tower room, as Irene sees it — though Curdie must wait to see it too.
Talk together: Curdie sees only a plain room, and Irene sees the wonder. Some people see lovely things sooner than others. Ask your child: what lovely things do you believe in that you cannot see?

'I cannot see her, princess,' he whispered, sorry and ashamed. 'Perhaps you are not meant to yet,' said Irene, taking his hand again. 'But the thread found you all the same. Grandmother says that is the main thing — being found, and finding.'

Then the two friends went down into the blue evening, and Curdie walked home over the snow to his mother, with his pickaxe on his shoulder and the mountain humming under his boots. And ever after, on clear nights, the miners said the tower window glowed a little, like a lamp lit over the whole mountain — for Irene, and Curdie, and everyone who was coming.
